t: The text traces the Solomonic dynasty, which ruled Ethiopia until 1974, to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba through their son Menelik I.
Modern scholarship considers its stories largely created to legitimise the dynasty's rise to power in the 13th century, while many Ethiopian Christians continue to regard it as historically reliable.
Its colophon gives a chain of translation from Coptic to Arabic to Geʽez, but many scholars doubt that a Coptic version ever existed.
dyk: In the story, Menelik asked Solomon for only a single tassel from the cloth covering the Ark of the Covenant, and Solomon gave him the entire thing; the young men travelling with him then smuggled the Ark out of the Temple.
ev: The Arabic translation named in the colophon is dated to this year
The start of the period 1314 to 1321–1322 that Conti Rossini, Littmann and Cerulli marked off for the composition of the book
Pedro Páez completes his História da Ethiópia, with a detailed translation of the Kebra Nagast through Menelek's return to Aksum
The third edition of James Bruce's Travels describes the contents of the manuscript he brought from Gondar
Carl Bezold publishes the entire text with commentary
E. A. Wallis Budge's English translation appears, in the first of two editions

f.made: Attributed to Nebure Id Yeshaq of Aksum; its colophon names a team of Ethiopian clerics who translated it into Geʽez from Arabic, in a tradition that gives Coptic as the first language
f.form: A composite prose work in Geʽez, divided into 117 chapters and framed as a debate of the 318 fathers of the First Council of Nicaea
f.where: Copies are held in libraries, among them a manuscript at the Bodleian Library (shelfmark Bruce 87), which James Bruce brought from Gondar
f.known: The Queen of Sheba (Makeda) and Solomon; Menelik I; the Ark of the Covenant coming to Ethiopia; the Solomonic dynasty's claimed descent; the debate of the 318 fathers; prophecies of Ethiopia's power
